Parcel position classification

Land valuation needs to know where each parcel sits on the street: a normal lot, a corner lot (Hook), a lot facing a T-junction (Tusuk Sate), or something else. The office's old buffer-based approach was only about 30–80% accurate, so I built a new rule-based method.

101,761
parcels classified
97.3%
weighted overall accuracy
200
stratified validation samples

How it works

  1. Extract each parcel's frontage, the edges that actually face a road.
  2. Find road intersections and measure the angle between road segments; angles between 25° and 155° count as a real corner.
  3. Apply class rules with clear definitions: dead ends and Y-junctions are not Tusuk Sate, lots with roads on both front and back are Normal, and Hook wins when a parcel qualifies for both.
  4. Validate with a stratified random sample of 50 parcels per class, checked visually against imagery, and summarize with a confusion matrix.
  5. Review the results with supervisors and apply their feedback: ignore footpaths, fix lots that have roads at both front and back, and record the class of the adjacent roads.
  6. Package the full workflow as a ModelBuilder model in ArcGIS Pro so it runs the same way every time.

The ModelBuilder model, in five stages

  1. Prepare parcelsCopy Features · Repair GeometryClean working copy of the parcel layer.
  2. Detect T-junctionsPairwise Buffer · Intersect · Summary StatisticsStem lines from T-junction points meet an inner buffer of each parcel; the nearest hit marks a Tusuk Sate candidate.
  3. Find road-facing sidesRoad-side analysis · Join FieldParcel edges that face a road become frontage segments, ranked by road class.
  4. Classify accessSelect · Calculate Field · MergeEach parcel is assigned Normal, Hook, Tusuk Sate or Others, then merged back.
  5. Attach attributesJoin · Calculate FieldsFrontage road class and frontage width are written to every parcel.

Surabaya surface temperature trends, by season

My thesis asked whether Surabaya's land surface is getting hotter, and whether the dry and rainy seasons behave differently. I split each year into seasons using BMKG's dasarian calendar and tested each series for a trend.

Trend test results (Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope)

SeriesSen's slopep-valueAt 95% confidence
Sentinel-3 LST, dry season+1.156 °C/yr0.064Not significant, close to threshold
Sentinel-3 LST, rainy season−0.109 °C/yr1.000No trend
BPS air temperature, dry season−0.094 °C/yr> 0.05Not significant
BPS air temperature, rainy season−0.150 °C/yr> 0.05Not significant

The dry season shows a warming signal that just misses significance, while the rainy season shows none. Satellite LST and station air temperature disagree in direction because they measure different things: radiant surface temperature versus air temperature. The record is also short, which is the main reason no trend reaches significance. I produced 16 seasonal LST maps and the two composite maps above.

Satu Peta Keputih

Keputih's official map did not yet cover every RT and RW boundary. Our team mapped the kelurahan's administrative boundaries, inventoried public facilities, and published everything in a web GIS for residents and the kelurahan office.

What I did

  • Ran the community survey and processed the population data for all nine RWs.
  • Mapped population density per RW and found a very uneven spread: a mean of 2,243.7 people per RW against a median of 1,378.
  • Ran hotspot analysis on the 39 facilities and an Ordinary Least Squares model relating facilities to population per RW in ArcGIS Pro.

Coal stockpile volume check

Mines estimate stockpile tonnage in different ways. We surveyed a stockpile with GNSS RTK, built a terrain model in Surpac, and compared the survey volume with the two figures the site already used: truck factor and weighbridge.

Three methods, one stockpile

At 1 t/m³ the survey volume equals about 3,438 t, within 0.5% of the weighbridge figure, so the survey works as an independent check. The truck factor came out about 8% lower and is only suitable for rough estimates.
